passage:
I'm Sangeeta, and I have lived across the landing from the Rao family for twelve years, so I've watched how it works in that flat. When the family shop slowed down, Siddharth's mother snapped at him for looking gloomy. When his sister's wedding budget grew, he was scolded for not helping enough. Everyone's worry seemed to land on him. His sister Meenal would look at her plate and say nothing.

Siddharth just smiles, takes the shopping bags and says, “I'll handle it.” I can't tell what he feels inside. Last week I found him sitting alone on the stairs for a long time. I asked if he wanted tea. “It's fine, Aunty,” he said. “They're just stressed.”

qa.q: How long has Sangeeta lived across the landing from the Rao family?
qa.a: Sangeeta has lived across the landing from the Rao family for twelve years.

qa.q: What does “They're just stressed” suggest about how Siddharth sees the situation?
qa.a: It suggests Siddharth excuses the family and swallows hurt to keep the peace, though the long time alone on the stairs hints at loneliness.

qa.q: What could Sangeeta do next that respects the family's privacy but shows care?
qa.a: Sangeeta could keep offering tea and an ear, and gently say that Siddharth does not have to handle everything alone.

qa.q: What might Meenal be feeling when looking at the plate and saying nothing?
qa.a: Meenal may feel guilty and helpless, since the wedding budget is part of the pressure, and speaking up might turn the blame toward Meenal as well.

grounding: A person living across the landing observes a stressed family blaming one adult child for tensions that belong to the whole household.

passage:
First Sunday. The shop had lost a big order, and dinner was tight. Amma set a dish down hard. “Parul, why are you always so slow to help? There's no peace in this house because of you.” Parul stared at her rice. Her older sister Vasudha kept eating.

Two weeks later. Parul had stopped telling anyone about her day. She came home from work, went straight to her room and answered “fine” to every question. At dinner Papa sighed, and Amma glanced her way.

A month on. Vasudha found Parul on the terrace. “It isn't you,” she said. “Money is tight, everyone is scared, and you're the one who gets it.” Parul's eyes filled. “I thought I was the problem.” “Let's talk to Amma and Papa together,” said Vasudha.

qa.q: What did Amma say to Parul at the first Sunday dinner?
qa.a: Amma said, “Parul, why are you always so slow to help? There's no peace in this house because of you.”

qa.q: Why did Parul say, “I thought I was the problem”?
qa.a: Parul had been blamed at dinner and glanced at for weeks, and nobody had said the tension came from the money worries.

qa.q: What choice did Vasudha make on the terrace that shifted things?
qa.a: Vasudha told Parul it was not Parul's fault and suggested talking to Amma and Papa together.

qa.q: What might Vasudha have felt during the first dinner, eating quietly while Parul was blamed?
qa.a: Vasudha may have felt uneasy and afraid of being blamed next, which could explain the silence, and the talk on the terrace hints at guilt.

grounding: In a stressed family one member is blamed for tensions that belong to the whole household, and feels unseen until an older sister names it.
